name: Emeka Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Emeka. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Hartleys at Long Meadow, a family farm, about four hundred hectares of wheat and beef cattle, and they do hay contracting for other farms in summer. I'm there at half six, feed the cattle, bed them down with straw, then whatever Mr Hartley needs: fencing, hauling bales, mending the cattle crush. I did twenty years in the army before this, so I'm good at early starts and doing as I'm told, but three years in I still don't know cattle like the Hartleys do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, you can see what you did at the end of the day. The Hartleys are good people, chapel people like us, and old Mr Hartley pays me better than most farms because he trusts me. The hard part is the knowledge, I can't read the weather or the animals yet. Tom, his son, is always on his tablet with the farm software, I leave all that to him.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Grace does the books for the chapel and two local businesses, part-time. Daniel's fifteen, Ruth's eleven. We've a mortgage, but my army pension pays most of it, and we've savings besides. I don't use any of this AI, I've got a basic phone and I'm happy with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently. Twenty years in the army taught me that the loudest new weapon is usually the one that jams first. People get excited about the latest thing and then the old ways carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays as it is, which is a good life. The Hartleys need hands, the pension's steady, Grace is busy. My only worry is that I'm slow to learn the cattle and one day Tom will want someone quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd ask Mr Hartley to let me shadow him at calving next spring. I'd keep the savings in the building society where they are, and keep giving to the chapel roof fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think Tom might want someone quicker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom said last month that I take twice as long to sort the heifers. He wasn't unkind, just honest. I'd rather hear it than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your faith say to you about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That work is good, and that we're not meant to worry about tomorrow. I'm better at the first than the second.

say: The **loudest new weapon** is usually the one that jams first.
People get excited and then the **old ways** carry on.
think: Life stays good: **steady pension**, Hartleys need hands, Grace is busy.
My worry is being **slow with cattle** while Tom wants someone quicker.
do: **Shadow** Mr Hartley at calving next spring.
**Keep giving** to the chapel roof fund.
S0.quote: Twenty years in the army taught me that the loudest new weapon is usually the one that jams first.
fieldNote: **Army pension** and savings give a very solid base.
His one worry is **skill**, voiced through Tom's honest comment.
**Faith** frames his outlook: work is good, worry less.

steps.text: Shadow Mr Hartley at calving next spring
Keep the savings in the building society untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say working with your hands is the safe place, always has been. I'd say it to Daniel especially, who wants to sit at a computer all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes in the shed. It's Grace I'd think about. My wife Grace has done the chapel's books by hand for twelve years, and I'd hate a machine to make her feel useless. Tom would bring in more software, but cattle still need bedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and wait to see what Tom actually brings in. I wouldn't rush to learn anything new. If Grace lost clients, we'd manage on my pay and the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, for Grace more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace if her clients started using software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace that the chapel will always want her, software or not, because people trust her. And I'd remind her we don't need the money, we need her happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel about computer jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a trade is worth more than a screen. An apprenticeship, electrician or mechanic. He'd roll his eyes. He's fifteen.

say: **Working with your hands** is the safe place, always has been.
He'd tell his son Daniel to choose a **trade**, not a screen.
think: The shed hardly changes, because **cattle still need** bedding whatever software Tom buys.
Grace's **bookkeeping** clients could move to software and dent her pride.
do: **Wait** to see what Tom brings in.
**Cover** any lost income from Grace with his pay and pension.
feel: A little **uneasy**, for Grace more than himself.
S1.quote: My wife Grace has done the chapel's books by hand for twelve years, and I'd hate a machine to make her feel useless.
fieldNote: Household exposure sits with **Grace's bookkeeping**, and her pride.
Pushes **apprenticeships** for his son, true to his traditional views.
Resistant: will **wait for Tom** rather than learn himself.

steps.text: Wait to see which software Tom brings to Long Meadow
Keep bedding and feeding the cattle as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other, because governments won't be ready. I'd say it at chapel, not online. And I'd say the free market will sort it eventually, but eventually is a long time for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 part hits Grace's books and Tom's planning, not me. By 2031 the robots can feed and bed cattle, and Tom would buy them, he's a modern man. But my army pension pays the mortgage, so the robots can take my job but they can't take my house. That's what I'd keep telling myself at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put every spare penny into savings and cut the second holiday. I'd ask my brother, who runs a security firm, whether there'd be work there. And I'd talk to the pastor about setting up a chapel group for men losing work, so nobody sits at home alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not for food, but for my place. A man without work isn't right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would three years' warning make you try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm forty-three, I'd be learning a thing that's taking my job. I'd rather spend the time finding where a pair of hands is still wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, then Mr Hartley himself, not Tom. Mr Hartley would tell me straight how long he could keep me.

say: **Families and churches** will have to look after each other.
The **free market** sorts it eventually, but that's a long time for a family.
think: By 2031 Tom would **buy robots** to feed and bed cattle.
His **army pension** covers the mortgage, so the house is safe.
do: **Save** every spare amount and cut the second holiday.
**Ask** his brother about work at the security firm.
**Start** a chapel group for men losing work.
feel: **Worried** for his place, not for food.
S2.quote: My army pension pays the mortgage, so the robots can take my job but they can't take my house.
fieldNote: Leans on **family and church**, not the state, as his outlook suggests.
Refuses AI tools even with **three years** of warning.
Identity is tied to **work**: “a man without work isn't right”.

steps.text: Put every spare amount into the building society account
Cut the family's second holiday of the year
Start a chapel group for men losing work
Ask his brother about jobs at the security firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep calm and keep working. There's time to prepare, and panic never helped a soldier or a farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time enough to pray on it, save for it, and see what the Hartleys (his bosses) decide. By 2034 Daniel's twenty-three and working, Ruth's nearly through school. I'd still lose the cattle job, probably, but at fifty-one, with less riding on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd wait. Keep saving at the usual rate, maybe a bit more. I'd keep working hard at Long Meadow so if the Hartleys keep one man on, it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but peaceful enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'one man kept on' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody to watch the robots and call the engineer, I suppose. Mr Hartley would want someone he trusts on the farm at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Grace see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would want a plan written down. I'd let her write it. She's better with paper than me.

say: **Keep calm** and keep working; there's time to prepare.
**Panic never helped** a soldier or a farmer, and it won't help now.
think: By 2034 the **children are grown**, so less rides on his job.
He'd still **probably lose** the cattle job at fifty-one.
do: **Wait** and watch what the Hartleys decide.
**Work hard** to be the one man kept on.
S3.quote: Five years is time enough to pray on it, save for it, and see what the Hartleys (his bosses) decide.
fieldNote: **Loyalty** to the Hartleys is his main plan.
Pictures himself as the **trusted night man** watching robots.
Hands planning to **Grace**, who wants it written down.

steps.text: Wait for the Hartleys' decision on robots before acting
Save a little more each month than usual
Work hard to be the one man kept at Long Meadow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and good families will use it to train their children in trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'll have given the Hartleys (his bosses) fifteen years, and I'd hope a family farm remembers that. I'd be fifty-six, the mortgage nearly gone, the pension still coming. I wouldn't worry much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, learn the cattle, keep saving. Make sure Daniel gets a proper apprenticeship. Nothing more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's in God's hands and ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What apprenticeship would you want for Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electrician, I think. Even robots need wiring. I'd pay for his tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about ten years that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Tom might not wait for the date. Young men like new things. But Mr Hartley will still be alive and still in charge, God willing.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of time for families to prepare.
Good families will use it to **train children** in proper trades.
think: By 2039 he'll have given **fifteen years** to the Hartleys.
With the **mortgage nearly gone** and the pension, he wouldn't worry much.
do: **Carry on** learning the cattle and keep saving as now.
**Pay** for Daniel's first set of tools himself.
feel: **Calm**, trusting God and the long horizon.
S4.quote: By 2039 I'll have given the Hartleys (his bosses) fifteen years, and I'd hope a family farm remembers that.
fieldNote: Long horizon plus **pension** removes nearly all worry.
His main act is for his son: an **electrician apprenticeship**.
Small doubt that **Tom** won't wait for the date.

steps.text: Keep learning the cattle at Long Meadow
Get Daniel an electrician apprenticeship and buy his tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Tom would have the robots in by 2031. What would help is apprenticeships for grown men, paid ones, so I could learn a trade without taking charity, and families and churches pulling together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What we teach our children. A man should earn his bread, and no robot is going to change what I teach my son.

headlineQuote: A man should earn his bread, and no robot is going to change what I teach my son.
portrait: Former **soldier** of twenty years, three years on a family beef and wheat farm.
An **army pension** pays most of the mortgage, so money is solid.
Chapel-going and **loyal** to the Hartleys; won't touch AI tools.
Calm in the plateau, **anxious** at AGI by 2028 as robots near the cattle sheds.
Leans on **family, faith** and apprenticeships, not government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Tom bringing robots in by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for grown men, without charity.
